tips.title: Hierarchical is tall, flat is wide
tips.body: A **hierarchical** structure has **many layers** and a **narrow span of control**. A **flat** structure has **few layers** and a **wide span**. The same staff, arranged differently — 81 people need 5 layers at a span of 3, but only 3 at a span of 9.

tips.title: Real Bosses Can Pay Fairly
tips.body: The five financial methods of motivation on the specification spell **RBCPF**: **R**emuneration, **B**onus, **C**ommission, **P**romotion, **F**ringe benefits. The three non-financial ones change the work, not the pay: **rotate** it (job rotation), **enrich** it (job enrichment), or hand over control of it (autonomy).

tips.title: Get them, keep them, get more from them
tips.body: Why motivation matters spells out as three verbs: **get** them (attracting employees), **keep** them (retaining employees), **get more from** them (productivity). A question on why motivation matters usually wants more than one, and the trio is the whole list on the specification.

tips.title: Centralised is about who decides
tips.body: **Hierarchical/flat** describes the **shape**. **Centralised/decentralised** describes **where decisions are made** — at the top, or pushed down to local managers. A business can be flat and centralised, or tall and decentralised. They are separate questions.

tips.title: Too much communication is also a problem
tips.body: The specification names **insufficient or excessive** communication. Too little causes mistakes; **too much** wastes time and buries the important message. Mentioning the excessive half is an easy mark most students miss.

tips.title: Job description describes the job
tips.body: A **job description** describes **the job** — duties and responsibilities. A **person specification** describes **the person** — skills and qualities needed. The names say which is which, so read them literally.

tips.title: Training links to retention, not just skill
tips.body: The specification asks for the **link between training, motivation and retention**. Trained staff are more capable *and* feel more valued, so they stay — which saves the cost of recruiting and training a replacement.

why.matters: A business is the people in it, and how they are arranged decides how fast a decision travels, whether a good idea reaches anyone who can act on it, and whether the best people stay. This topic is the shape of a business (tall or flat), how it fills a job and trains the person who gets it, and what actually makes people work well — which is not only pay, and is cheapest when it is not.

examples.title: Eighty-one staff, five layers or three
examples.body:
Fernhill has **81** frontline staff. If each manager looks after **3** people (a narrow span of control), it needs 27 supervisors, 9 managers, 3 senior managers and a director: **five layers**, and a message from the top passes through four people before it reaches the shop floor.

With a span of **9** it needs 9 managers and a director: **three layers**, 30 fewer salaries and a shorter chain — but each manager has nine people to know. Same staff, two shapes.

visual.alt: A table of the layers needed for eighty-one frontline staff: five layers of one, three, nine, twenty-seven and eighty-one at a span of three, against three layers of one, nine and eighty-one at a span of nine

examples.title: The lifeguard advert
examples.body:
The **job description** says what the job is: supervise the pool, respond to emergencies, check the water each morning. The **person specification** says who can do it: a current lifeguard qualification, calm under pressure, able to work weekends.

The candidate's **CV** and **application form** are their side of the same conversation. Get the two business documents the wrong way round in an exam and the answer describes a person as if they were a list of duties.

visual.alt: A table of recruitment documents: the job description describes the lifeguard's duties, the person specification describes the qualification and qualities needed, and the CV and application form come from the applicant

examples.title: Why the phone shop pays commission
examples.body:
A phone shop pays its Saturday staff **commission** on every contract sold: pay follows effort, and the shop can see the effort in the sales figures. A hospital cannot pay a nurse per patient, so it motivates with the work itself — responsibility, training, a say in the rota: **autonomy** and **job enrichment**.

Financial methods work where output can be counted and the money is there; non-financial ones work everywhere, cost less and wear off more slowly. Fernhill, with thin margins, is nearer the hospital than the phone shop.

visual.alt: Four boxes around what makes people work well: pay that follows effort such as commission and bonus, pay that rewards staying such as promotion and fringe benefits, interesting work through job rotation and enrichment, and being trusted through autonomy

steps.title: Organisational structures
steps.body:
**An organisational structure sets out who reports to whom.** Two pairs of terms describe it, and they answer **different** questions.

**Hierarchical against flat — the shape.**

A **hierarchical** structure has **many layers** and a **narrow span of control** — each manager supervises few people. A **flat** structure has **few layers** and a **wide span** — each manager supervises many.

**Span of control** is how many people report directly to one manager, and it is what decides the shape. *Fernhill Garden Centres* has **81** frontline staff. At a span of **3**, the structure runs 81 → 27 → 9 → 3 → 1 — **5 layers**. At a span of **9**, it runs 81 → 9 → 1 — just **3**.

**Hierarchical**: close supervision, clear promotion ladder, defined roles. But it is **expensive** in managers, decisions travel **slowly** up and down, and messages get distorted passing through layers.

**Flat**: fewer managers so **lower costs**, **faster** communication, and staff with more responsibility. But each manager is stretched, supervision is lighter, and there are **fewer promotions** to offer.

**Centralised against decentralised — who decides.**

**Centralised**: decisions are made at the **top**. Consistent across the business, tight control, and senior experience applied everywhere — but slow, and local knowledge is wasted.

**Decentralised**: decisions are pushed **down** to local managers. Faster, responsive to local conditions, and motivating for those given the authority — but less consistent, and it relies on local managers being good.

**These are separate choices.** A business can be flat and centralised, or hierarchical and decentralised.

steps.title: Communication
steps.body:
**The specification asks for the impact of insufficient or excessive communication on efficiency and motivation.** Both directions, and both effects.

**Insufficient communication.** Staff do not know what is expected, so work is duplicated or missed and mistakes are made — **efficiency falls**. They also feel uninformed and unimportant, and hear about changes affecting them through rumour, so **motivation falls**.

**Excessive communication** is the half students forget, and it is just as real. Time spent reading messages and sitting in meetings is time not spent working, so **efficiency falls**. Worse, the message that matters is **buried** among those that do not, so important information gets missed precisely because there is so much of it. Staff who are constantly interrupted also find it harder to concentrate, which affects **motivation**.

**Barriers to effective communication:**

- **Too many layers** — the message is distorted as it passes down, which is a hierarchical structure's built-in weakness.
- **Jargon or technical language** the receiver does not understand.
- **The wrong medium** — a complex change sent by text, or a one-line fact given a meeting.
- **Physical distance**, including remote working and staff spread across sites.
- **Noise and distraction**, literal or otherwise.
- **Poor relationships**, where staff do not feel able to ask or to disagree.

**For Fernhill** the barriers are mostly structural: staff spread across several garden centres, many part-time and not present when announcements are made, and seasonal workers who were never included in the usual channels.

check.prompt: What is one problem caused by excessive communication?
options: Managers cannot pass instructions down to staff
Staff never find out about changes that directly affect them
Work is duplicated because nobody knows their role

check.solution: Too much communication **buries** what matters and consumes time that could be spent working. The other three are problems of **insufficient** communication.

steps.title: Ways of working
steps.body:
**The specification covers hours, contracts and the effect of technology.**

**Hours.** **Full-time** and **part-time** are the basic split. **Flexible hours** let staff vary when they work — useful for people with caring responsibilities, and useful to the business at busy times.

**Contracts.** A **permanent** contract has no end date, giving the employee security and the business continuity and a reason to invest in training. A **temporary** contract runs for a fixed period, which suits seasonal work and lets the business adjust its costs — but the employee has no security, may be less committed, and is more likely to leave. A **freelance** worker is self-employed and paid per job: the business pays only for work done and owes no holiday or sick pay, but has less control and no guarantee the person is available next time.

**For Fernhill this is the central HR decision.** Garden centres are intensely seasonal — spring is frantic and January is quiet. **Temporary** and **part-time** contracts let it match staffing to demand instead of paying a full-time workforce through a quiet winter. The cost is that seasonal staff know less about the products, need training every year, and have little reason to be loyal.

**The impact of technology on ways of working** is framed by the specification as **efficiency** and **remote working**.

**Efficiency**: tasks are automated, information is found faster, and staff can be rostered and coordinated more precisely.

**Remote working**: people can work from anywhere. That widens the pool of applicants, cuts the need for office space and commuting, and often improves work-life balance. Against that, it makes communication harder, weakens team relationships, and makes some staff harder to supervise — and for a garden centre, most jobs cannot be done remotely at all.

steps.title: Job roles and recruitment
steps.body:
**The specification names five levels of job role.**

**Directors** set the **aims and objectives** and make the major decisions about the business as a whole.

**Senior managers** turn those objectives into plans and are responsible for large areas or departments.

**Supervisors and team leaders** oversee the day-to-day work of a small team and are the first point of contact for the people doing the job.

**Operational staff** do the work the business exists to do — serving customers, growing plants, running tills.

**Support staff** keep the business running behind that: finance, IT, human resources, administration.

**Recruitment documents.** The names say what each is, so read them literally.

- A **job description** describes **the job**: title, duties, responsibilities, who it reports to.
- A **person specification** describes **the person**: skills, qualifications, experience and qualities needed.
- An **application form** is written by the business, so every applicant answers the **same questions** and can be compared directly.
- A **CV** is written by the applicant, so it shows what **they** choose to present — and how well they present it.

**Internal recruitment** fills the post from existing staff. It is **cheaper and faster**, the person is **known** and already understands the business, and the promotion **motivates** others. But it brings **no new ideas**, and it leaves **another vacancy** to fill.

**External recruitment** brings in someone from outside: **new ideas and experience**, a **wider field** of applicants, and no gap left elsewhere. But it is **slower and more expensive**, the person is **unknown**, they need **induction**, and passing over internal candidates can **demotivate** them.

steps.title: Training and development
steps.body:
**How businesses train**, as the specification lists it:

**Formal training** is structured and planned — a course, a qualification, a scheduled session. It is thorough and can be certificated, but it costs money and takes people away from work.

**Informal training** happens on the job, by watching and being shown. It is cheap and immediately relevant, but it is inconsistent, and bad habits pass on as easily as good ones.

**Self-learning** is the employee teaching themselves — reading, online material, practice. Cheap and flexible, but it depends on motivation and there is nobody to correct a misunderstanding.

**Ongoing training for all employees** matters because training is not something done once at induction. Products, systems and rules change, and everyone needs to keep up.

**Target setting and performance reviews** are how development is directed. A review looks at how someone is doing, agrees what to improve, and sets targets to work towards before the next one.

**Why businesses train**, which is where the marks are.

**The specification asks for the link between training, motivation and retention.** Training makes staff more **capable**, so quality and productivity rise. It also makes them feel **valued** and shows a path forward, so they are **more motivated** — and motivated, capable staff are **less likely to leave**.

**Retention saves real money.** Fernhill has **120** staff. If **30** leave in a year, turnover is **25%**. After investing in training, **12** leave — turnover of **10%**, and **18 fewer people** to recruit, induct and train from scratch.

(Staff turnover as a percentage is not a formula on the specification; it is used here only to put a number on retention.)

**Retraining to use new technology** is named separately. Buying equipment achieves nothing if nobody can use it — the training is part of the investment, not an optional extra.

steps.body: **The specification asks why motivation matters and how businesses achieve it**, splitting the methods into financial and non-financial.

steps.text: Motivation matters for three reasons the specification names: **attracting** employees, **retaining** them, and **productivity**

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
*Fernhill Garden Centres* has 120 staff across several sites, many part-time or seasonal. It has 81 frontline staff and 30 people left last year.

**Part A.**

1. What is meant by span of control?
2. Name the four recruitment documents.
3. Name three non-financial methods of motivation.

**Part B.**

4. Explain the difference between a hierarchical and a flat structure.
5. Calculate Fernhill's staff turnover.
6. Explain the difference between a job description and a person specification.

**Part C.**

7. Explain two problems that **excessive** communication could cause at Fernhill.
8. Explain why Fernhill uses temporary contracts, and one drawback of doing so.
9. Recommend how Fernhill could reduce its staff turnover, and justify your answer.

For question 9, remember its margins are thin — a large pay rise may not be available.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Keep the two pairs of terms apart.** **Hierarchical/flat** is the **shape**; **centralised/decentralised** is **who decides**. They are independent, and a business can be flat and centralised. Treating them as the same pair is a common and costly confusion.

**Use the span of control to explain the shape.** A narrow span means **more layers** for the same staff — 81 people need 5 layers at a span of 3 but only 3 at a span of 9. That single comparison explains why hierarchical structures cost more in managers and communicate more slowly.

**Mention excessive communication.** The specification says **insufficient or excessive**, and almost every answer covers only the first. Too much communication **buries** the important message and consumes working time — an easy mark sitting unclaimed.

**Read the recruitment documents literally.** The **job description** describes the **job**; the **person specification** describes the **person**. Note also who writes what: the **application form** is the business's, so candidates can be compared on the same questions; the **CV** is the candidate's, so it shows what they choose to present.

**Link training to retention, not just to skill.** The specification asks for the link between **training, motivation and retention**. Trained staff are more capable **and** feel more valued, so fewer leave — and each leaver avoided saves recruiting, inducting and training a replacement. Cutting turnover from 25% to 10% is 18 fewer replacements a year.

**Explain why non-financial methods often work better.** A pay rise is quickly absorbed into what feels normal, and it must be paid again every year. **Autonomy**, **job enrichment** and **job rotation** cost little and do not wear off in the same way. For a business with thin margins this is the practical answer, not a second-best one.

**Apply it to the business.** A garden centre is **seasonal**, so **temporary** and **part-time** contracts match staffing to demand — and the cost is staff who know the products less well and have little reason to be loyal. That is application, and it is what the levels reward.

**Judge, and say what it depends on.** *Fernhill should use non-financial methods because its margins cannot support a pay rise, provided pay is already at the market rate* is a conclusion. If pay is **below** the market rate, no amount of job enrichment will fix it — and saying so shows real judgement.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Span of control** is how many report directly to one manager.
- **Hierarchical**: many layers, narrow span — costly, slower, more promotion rungs.
- **Flat**: few layers, wide span — cheaper, faster, fewer promotions.
- 81 staff need **5 layers** at a span of 3, but **3** at a span of 9.
- **Centralised**: decisions at the top. **Decentralised**: decisions pushed down.
- Shape and decision-making are **separate** choices.
- **Insufficient** communication causes mistakes and makes staff feel unvalued.
- **Excessive** communication wastes time and **buries** what matters.
- Barriers: too many layers, jargon, the wrong medium, distance, noise, poor relationships.
- Contracts: **permanent**, **temporary**, **freelance**; hours: full-time, part-time, **flexible**.
- Technology affects **efficiency** and enables **remote working**.
- Roles: **directors, senior managers, supervisors, operational staff, support staff**.
- **Job description** describes the job; **person specification** describes the person.
- **Internal** recruitment is cheaper and known; **external** brings new ideas.
- Motivation matters for **attracting**, **retaining** and **productivity**.
- **Financial**: remuneration, bonus, commission, promotion, fringe benefits. **Non-financial**: job rotation, job enrichment, autonomy.

questions.prompt: Fernhill Garden Centres employs 120 staff across several sites, many part-time or on temporary seasonal contracts. Last year 30 staff left. Its profit margins are thin. The owners are considering two ways to cut staff turnover. Option 1: a 5% pay rise for all staff. Option 2: a training programme, with more autonomy for experienced staff. Justify which option Fernhill should choose.
questions.solution:
Fernhill's staff turnover is $(30 \div 120) \times 100 = \textbf{25\%}$ — one worker in four leaving each year. That is costly: every leaver must be **recruited, inducted and trained**, and during the weeks before a replacement is useful the remaining staff carry the work.

**The causes are visible in how the business is organised.** Much of the workforce is **temporary and seasonal**, and a temporary contract offers no security and little reason to be loyal, so some of that 25% is designed into the staffing model rather than being a failure of management. The business is also **multi-site** and heavily **part-time**, so staff may feel disconnected — part-time workers are often absent when announcements are made and can end up outside the normal channels of communication altogether.

**Training is the strongest lever available.** The specification links **training, motivation and retention** directly: trained staff are more **capable**, so the work goes better, and they feel **valued** and can see a path forward, so they are more likely to stay. For a garden centre this is doubly useful, because plant knowledge is exactly what customers come in for — so the training that keeps staff also improves the service.

**Non-financial motivation suits this business particularly well** because its **margins are thin**. **Autonomy** — letting experienced staff choose planting displays or reorganise their section — costs nothing and gives real ownership of the work. **Job enrichment** and **job rotation** add variety and challenge, which matters in a role that could otherwise be repetitive. These methods are cheap, and their effect does not wear off the way a pay rise does once it becomes the new normal.

**Better communication would also help.** With staff across several sites and many working part-time, it is easy for people to feel peripheral. Making sure part-time and seasonal staff are actually included — not merely sent messages — addresses the sense of being an afterthought that drives people out.

The chain worth following is this: better training and more autonomy → staff feel more capable and valued → **fewer leave** → turnover falls from 25% towards, say, 10%, which is **18 fewer people to replace each year** → recruitment and training costs fall, and the staff who remain know the products better → **better customer service** → more repeat custom and higher revenue. The saving is not only the recruitment cost; it is the expertise that stops walking out of the door.

**Option 1, a 5% pay rise for everyone,** costs money every year on thin margins, and a rise that goes to all 120 staff rewards the people who were staying anyway as much as those about to leave. It is also quickly treated as normal, so its effect fades.

**Recommendation: Option 2.** Training and autonomy fit both Fernhill's financial position and the nature of the work. But this depends on **pay already being near the market rate**: if Fernhill pays less than the garden centre down the road, no amount of job enrichment will hold staff, and Option 1 would have to come first.

It should also accept that **some turnover is unavoidable and even appropriate**. Seasonal contracts exist because demand is seasonal, and students and temporary workers will always move on. The realistic target is to retain the **permanent, knowledgeable core** — not to drive 25% to zero, which would mean abandoning the flexible staffing that makes a seasonal business affordable at all.

questions.prompt: Fernhill Garden Centres has 81 frontline staff and is considering moving from a hierarchical structure with a span of control of 3 to a flatter structure with a span of 9, and decentralising decisions to individual site managers. Evaluate whether Fernhill should make these changes.
questions.solution:
These are **two separate changes**, and it is worth treating them separately because a business can adopt either without the other. The **shape** of the structure and **who makes decisions** are independent questions.

**The change in shape.** With **81** frontline staff and a span of control of **3**, the structure runs 81 → 27 → 9 → 3 → 1, which is **five layers**. Widening the span to **9** gives 81 → 9 → 1 — just **three layers**.

The immediate saving is in **managers**. Two entire layers of management disappear, and each of those posts is a salary, so the wage bill falls appreciably. For a business described as having **thin margins**, that is a substantial and permanent reduction in fixed costs.

**Communication should also improve.** A message currently passes through five layers between the top and the shop floor, and is distorted a little at each one — the specification names too many layers as a barrier to effective communication. With three layers, instructions arrive faster and more accurately, and information travels back up more readily too.

**The costs of flattening.** Each manager would supervise **nine** people rather than three, which is far less individual attention. New and seasonal staff — of whom Fernhill has many — need more supervision than experienced ones, so a wide span is hardest precisely where this business is weakest. Overstretched managers also make poorer decisions and are themselves at risk of leaving.

There are **fewer promotions** too. Removing two layers removes two rungs of the ladder, and promotion is one of the financial motivators the specification names. For a business already losing **25%** of its staff a year, reducing the visible ways to progress works against retention at exactly the wrong moment.

**Decentralising decisions** is the stronger of the two proposals for this particular business. Fernhill operates across **several sites**, and a garden centre's trade depends on **local conditions** — the weather, the soil, what sells in that area, when the local schools break up. A site manager can respond to those far faster than a head office can. Decentralising also **motivates** the managers themselves, since **autonomy** is a non-financial motivator and a powerful one.

The risks are **inconsistency** between sites and dependence on the **quality of each site manager**. If one manager makes poor buying decisions, head office may not notice until the stock is unsold. A business with high turnover may also have site managers who are relatively new to the role.

**Conclusion.** Fernhill should **decentralise, and flatten more cautiously**.

Decentralising fits the business almost perfectly: it is multi-site, it is seasonal, its trade is local, and the change costs nothing while motivating the managers it affects. The risks are real but manageable through clear limits on what site managers may decide and regular reporting back.

Flattening from five layers to three in one step is more than this business should take on at once. The cost saving is attractive, but a span of **nine** over a largely part-time and seasonal workforce risks supervision failing where it is most needed, and removing promotion rungs while turnover is already at 25% could make that worse. Removing **one** layer rather than two would capture much of the saving and the faster communication while leaving spans manageable.

What the decision ultimately depends on is the **experience of the staff being supervised**. If Fernhill's frontline is mostly long-serving and knowledgeable, a wide span is perfectly workable. If it is largely seasonal and new each spring — which the 25% turnover suggests — then close supervision is doing necessary work, and removing it to save management salaries would cost more in service quality and mistakes than it saves in wages.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following job roles is responsible for the day-to-day supervision of a small team of operational staff?
questions.solution: The specification names the key job roles as directors, senior managers, supervisors or team leaders, and operational and support staff. Directors set the strategy, senior managers run departments and carry it out, supervisors or team leaders organise and check the daily work of a small team, operational staff do that work, and support staff (such as IT or administration) help the others do theirs.
options: Supervisor or team leader
One of the company's directors
A senior manager
A member of support staff

questions.prompt: A web design business pays a photographer for one day's work on a single project. She is not an employee and also works for other businesses. Which one of the following best describes her contract?
questions.solution: A **freelance** contract pays someone who is not an employee to do a specific piece of work; she sells her time to several businesses. The specification pairs it with permanent and temporary contracts. Full-time and flexible hours describe how many hours an employee works and when, not whether they are employed at all.
options: Freelance
Permanent
Full-time
Flexible hours

questions.prompt: An engineer emails a report full of technical jargon to the sales team, who cannot follow it and so give customers wrong information. Which one of the following best describes the problem?
questions.solution: The message was sent, and it was not too long or too frequent, so this is neither excessive nor insufficient communication: it is a **barrier**, language the receiver cannot understand. Other barriers are noise, distance, poor technology and a receiver who is not listening. The effect is the one the specification highlights: efficiency falls, because work is done wrongly, and staff are frustrated.
options: A barrier to effective communication
An example of excessive communication
An example of insufficient communication
The result of a manager's wide span of control

questions.prompt: A chain of garden centres lets each site's manager choose which plants to stock and what to charge for them. Why might this decentralised approach suit the chain?
questions.solution: Decentralised means decisions are taken away from the centre, by the people closest to the customer. Plants that sell in a seaside town differ from those that sell inland, and a local manager sees that at once, so each site stocks and prices what its own customers want and sells more. The cost is consistency: sites will differ, which is exactly what a centralised chain avoids. Head office and training are still needed.

markScheme.description: each site can match stock and prices to its local customers

options: Head office no longer needs to employ any senior managers at all
Each site can match its stock and prices to its own local customers
All sites will then stock identical plants at prices set by head office's buyers
Site managers no longer need any training to do their jobs

questions.prompt: Give the name of the document in which a job applicant sets out their own qualifications, experience and skills.
questions.solution: A **CV** (curriculum vitae). The four recruitment documents on the specification are the job description (what the post involves), the person specification (the skills and qualities the business wants), the application form (the business's own questions) and the CV (the applicant's own account of themselves).

questions.prompt: A business has 48 operational staff. Each supervisor has 6 operational staff reporting to them, and each manager has 4 supervisors reporting to them. Calculate the number of managers the business needs.
questions.solution: Work up the hierarchy one layer at a time. Supervisors: $48 \div 6 = 8$. Managers: $8 \div 4 = 2$. The structure has three layers: 48 operational staff, 8 supervisors and 2 managers. Widening the spans of control, so that more staff report to each supervisor, would need fewer supervisors and managers and make the structure flatter.

questions.prompt: A salesperson is paid a basic salary of £1,600 a month plus commission of 5% of the value of everything she sells. In one month she sells £24,000 of goods. Calculate her total pay for the month.
questions.solution: Commission $= 5\% \times 24000 = 0.05 \times 24000 = £1200$. Total pay $=$ basic salary $+$ commission $= 1600 + 1200 = £2800$. Commission is a financial method of motivation: the more she sells, the more she earns, so the business pays most in the months it earns most.

questions.prompt: A business has 150 staff, and 45 of them leave each year. Recruiting and training each replacement costs the business £2,000. A training and development programme costing £30,000 a year is expected to cut the number of leavers to 24. Calculate the net saving the programme would make in its first year, after its own cost has been paid.
questions.solution: Cost of replacing leavers now $= 45 \times 2000 = £90000$. With the programme: $24 \times 2000 = £48000$ of replacement costs plus £30,000 for the programme $= £78000$. Saving $= 90000 - 78000 = £12000$. Staff turnover falls from $45 \div 150 \times 100 = 30\%$ to $24 \div 150 \times 100 = 16\%$, which is the link the specification draws between training, motivation and retention.

questions.prompt: Explain one benefit to a business of holding regular performance reviews with its employees.
questions.solution: One point in a chain. A performance review shows where an employee is doing well and where they need to improve, so targets and training can be agreed, so the employee's work improves and productivity rises. A second route: being reviewed and set targets makes the employee feel the business is investing in them, so they are more motivated and more likely to stay.

markScheme.description: benefit identified: a review shows where an employee needs to improve, so targets or training can be agreed

criteria.text: A benefit named: a review shows where an employee is doing well or needs to improve, so targets or training can be agreed
Developed: the employee knows what is expected and gets the training to do it
Developed to an outcome: their work improves, so productivity rises, or they feel valued and stay

questions.modelAnswer: A performance review lets a manager and an employee look together at how the employee is doing and agree targets for the next period. This means any weakness is picked up early and training can be arranged to deal with it, so the employee's work improves and productivity rises, rather than the problem being noticed only when a customer complains.

questions.prompt: Discuss the impact on a business of using job enrichment to motivate its employees.
questions.solution: Two chains. For: job enrichment gives an employee more challenging work and more responsibility, so the work itself becomes satisfying, so motivation rises without a rise in pay, and motivated staff are more productive and less likely to leave. Against: an enriched job needs training and trust, and an employee given responsibility without support can feel overloaded, so quality or morale falls; some staff want a simple job and a pay rise rather than more responsibility. A strong answer says the impact depends on the employee and on the work.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain of reasoning
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each reaching an outcome for a business

criteria.text: Job enrichment makes the work itself more satisfying, developed to an outcome for productivity, retention or the wage bill
Enrichment needs training and suits some employees and jobs better than others, developed to an outcome such as overload or falling quality
Reasoning uses the terms of the specification (non-financial motivation, productivity, retention) and reaches a view on what the impact depends on

questions.modelAnswer: Job enrichment gives an employee more challenging work and more responsibility: a shop assistant who is given charge of ordering stock for one department, for example, instead of only filling shelves. The work itself becomes more satisfying, so the employee is motivated without the business paying more, and a motivated employee works harder, makes fewer mistakes and is less likely to leave, which saves the cost of recruiting and training a replacement. The impact is not all positive. An enriched job needs training and trust, and an employee given responsibility without the skills or support to carry it can feel overloaded, so quality falls and the employee becomes less motivated rather than more. Not every employee wants it either: some prefer a simple job done well and a pay rise, and for them enrichment feels like extra work for the same money. Its impact therefore depends on matching the enrichment to the employee and backing it with training, and on the nature of the work, since a job on a production line is harder to enrich than one serving customers.

questions.prompt: Thornby Logistics runs a parcel depot with 60 operational staff and three supervisors. Its depot manager is leaving, and the business is about to install a new computerised routing system that none of its staff has used. It has written a job description and a person specification for the post; the person specification asks for experience of computerised routing systems. Option 1: promote one of the three supervisors to depot manager. Option 2: recruit externally, which would cost £6,000 in advertising and agency fees and take about three months. Justify which option Thornby Logistics should choose.
questions.solution: Choose, argue both ways, name the deciding factor. External: the person specification will ask for experience of routing systems that no supervisor has, so a manager who has run one elsewhere brings that knowledge from the first day and new ideas with it; £6,000 and three months are one-off costs against a post that decides how 60 staff and the new system perform. Internal: quicker, cheaper, a known person who knows the staff and the site, and a promotion that motivates the other supervisors; but it leaves a supervisor vacancy and the new manager would be learning the system and the job at once. Judgement: the timing of the new system decides it; if the supplier's training could close the gap before it goes live, promote internally.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 3): limited points, little application, no real judgement
Level 2 (4 to 6): developed reasoning for the choice with some application; a judgement is made
Level 3 (7 to 9): developed reasoning for the choice and against the alternative, applied throughout, with a justified judgement that names the deciding factor

criteria.text: A clear choice with developed reasons applied to Thornby's new routing system, its three supervisors and the £6,000 and three months
Developed reasons against the alternative, applied to the case
A judgement naming the deciding factor: the timing of the new system, the skills gap in the person specification, or the vacancy a promotion leaves behind

questions.modelAnswer: Thornby Logistics should choose Option 2 and recruit externally. The deciding problem is the new routing system: the person specification will ask for experience of computerised routing, and none of the three supervisors has it. A manager recruited from a depot that already runs such a system brings that knowledge on the day they start, so the system goes live under someone who has seen it work, and they bring ideas from another business about how a depot should run. The cost of £6,000 and the three-month wait are real, but they are one-off costs against a post that decides how well sixty staff and the new system perform every day. Promoting a supervisor would be quicker and cheaper, the person is already known and knows the staff, the site and the customers, and seeing a colleague promoted motivates the other two; but it creates a supervisor vacancy that still has to be filled, and the new manager would be learning the routing system from scratch at the same time as learning to manage, which is when mistakes with customers' parcels are most likely. The deciding factor is timing: the system arrives soon and the depot needs someone who already understands it. If the system's supplier offered a training course that a supervisor could complete before it goes live, internal promotion would become the better choice, because the knowledge gap would close and Thornby would keep the £6,000 and the three months.

questions.prompt: Carrick Insurance employs 60 office staff in a city-centre office, all full-time and permanent, who handle customers' claims by phone and email. Last year 18 staff left, and the business struggled to recruit replacements because rivals offer home working. Its office lease costs £180,000 a year and expires next year. The owners propose letting all staff work from home three days a week on flexible hours, and moving to a smaller office. Evaluate whether Carrick Insurance should make this change.
questions.solution: Both sides, applied, then what it depends on. For: turnover of 30% and failed recruitment are the pressing problem, and home working with flexible hours is what the rivals offer, so it should help Carrick retain and attract staff; the work is phone and email, which technology lets staff do anywhere; the lease expiring next year makes the saving on the £180,000 real. Against: claims work is learned informally from the person next to you and involves confidential information, so insufficient communication and weaker supervision can mean mistakes with customers' claims; team spirit and some staff's motivation can fall; flexible hours must still cover the times customers ring. Judgement: it depends on whether the speed and accuracy of claims can be measured remotely and communication kept up; on balance yes, with fixed office days, because the staffing problem threatens the business more.

Level 2 (5 to 8): mostly accurate knowledge with terminology in places, sound application to the business though not always consistent, chains of reasoning that connect points, and a conclusion based on sound evaluation

Level 3 (9 to 12): accurate knowledge and terminology throughout, detailed application to the business throughout, detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning, and a valid, well-reasoned conclusion

criteria.text: Reaches level 1: some accurate knowledge of ways of working or communication, applied at least a little to Carrick, with a conclusion of some kind
Reaches level 2: sound application to Carrick's turnover, its recruitment problem, the £180,000 lease and the nature of claims work, with chains of reasoning and a supported conclusion

Reaches level 3: accurate and detailed throughout, with logical chains linking retention, efficiency, communication and motivation, and a well-reasoned conclusion that says what the decision depends on

questions.modelAnswer: Carrick has a recruitment and retention problem: 18 of 60 staff left last year, a turnover of 30%, and the business cannot replace them because rivals offer what it does not. Home working three days a week with flexible hours answers that directly. Staff who no longer commute every day and can fit work around their lives are more likely to stay, and the business can recruit from people who live too far from the city centre to work there five days a week. Technology makes the work possible from home: claims are handled by phone and email, which need a laptop and a connection, not a desk in the city. The lease expiring next year makes the saving real: a smaller office for staff who are in two days a week could cut a large part of the £180,000 a year, and that saving can fund the equipment and the pay rivals offer. The risks are about communication and control. Claims work involves judgement and confidential information, and a new member of staff learns it informally by asking the person next to them; at home that person is a message away, so insufficient communication leads to mistakes with customers' claims and slower training. Supervisors cannot see who is struggling, team spirit is harder to build, and some staff will not have a quiet place to work or will feel isolated, so their motivation can fall. Flexible hours also mean the business must make sure enough people are working when customers ring. Whether Carrick should make the change depends on whether it can keep communication and quality up remotely: fixed office days for the whole team, a daily call, and measuring the speed and accuracy of claims handled rather than hours at a desk. On balance it should, because the problem it faces now, that it cannot keep or recruit staff, threatens the business more than the problems of remote working, which can be managed, and the lease expiry gives it a one-off chance to capture the saving. The deciding factor is whether the quality of claims handling can be monitored from a distance; if it cannot, Carrick should start with two days at home rather than three.

examTechnique.body:
Keep **hierarchical/flat** (the shape) apart from **centralised/decentralised** (who decides) — they are independent. Use the **span of control** to explain why a structure has the layers it does.

Cover **excessive** as well as insufficient communication. Link **training to retention**, not just to skill, and apply every point to the **business in the question**.
examinerErrors: Treating flat and decentralised as the same thing.
Describing layers without mentioning the span of control.
Covering only insufficient communication and not excessive.
Swapping the job description and the person specification.
Linking training to skill alone, not to motivation and retention.
Recommending a pay rise without considering what the business can afford.
Giving generic HR points with no reference to the business in the question.
Ending with "there are advantages and disadvantages" and no judgement.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer separates the **shape** of a structure from **who makes the decisions**, and uses the **span of control** to show why — 81 staff need five layers at a span of 3 but three at a span of 9. It covers **excessive** communication as well as insufficient, and links **training to motivation and retention** with a figure attached. It chooses motivation methods the business can actually **afford**, noting that non-financial methods are cheap and do not wear off. Every point names the business — **seasonal**, **multi-site**, **part-time** — and it closes with a **judgement that names what it depends on**, such as whether pay is already at the market rate.
